feedback.pattern: Sustained assertion error in iterator traversal logic
feedback.explanation: This test has failed consistently across runs 26–40 with evolving error messages: a NullPointerException on the flags stack in run 26, an assertion error (expected 2, got 1) in run 27, and an assertion error (expected 2, got null) in run 29. A code change at run 40 (3 lines removed, 13 added) occurred after the test began failing but did not result in a passing test. The error messages shifted from null-pointer to assertion mismatches across the runs, indicating changes to the iterator implementation occurred between runs 26 and 40. The test has remained failing through run 40.
nextSteps: Examine the iterator's hasNext() and next() methods to ensure they correctly traverse the BST in in-order (left, root, right) sequence; a common mistake is forgetting to push the right subtree onto the stack after visiting a node, or visiting nodes in the wrong order.

Manually trace through a small BST (e.g., 3 nodes: root with left and right children) using your iterator code step-by-step, writing down the stack state and the order of nodes returned by next(), to identify where the traversal deviates from the expected in-order sequence.

Check that the iterator correctly handles the transition from processing the left subtree to the root to the right subtree; if using a stack-based approach, verify that you push the right child only after the root has been visited, not before.

feedback.pattern: Sustained logic error in non-BST search implementation
feedback.explanation: This test has failed consistently since run 3 with the assertion error (expected true, got false). The containsNonBST method was implemented in run 9 (20 lines added). The test continued to fail through run 40 with no further changes to the method. The consistent failure across all runs indicates the method implementation has not been modified since run 9, and the test has remained in a failing state.
nextSteps: Rewrite containsNonBST to perform a full tree traversal (visiting every node) rather than using BST comparison logic; use a helper method that recursively checks the current node and then searches both left and right subtrees unconditionally, returning true if any node matches the target value.

Test your implementation on a deliberately non-BST tree (e.g., a tree where the right child of the root is smaller than the root) to confirm it finds values that a BST search would miss due to incorrect pruning.

Distinguish clearly between contains (which can assume BST ordering and prune branches) and containsNonBST (which must check all nodes); consider adding a comment in the code to remind yourself of this difference.

feedback.explanation: This test has failed consistently since its introduction in run 45 with a size assertion error. The test remained failing through run 52. The diff at run 55 shows substantial changes to the remove method implementation, which correlates with the test transitioning from failing to passing.
nextSteps: Verify that your remove method decrements the size counter exactly once per successful removal, and only when a node is actually deleted (not when a recursive call returns null or when a node is restructured without being removed).

Test your remove method with a sequence of removals on a larger tree (e.g., remove multiple nodes including some with two children) and print the size after each removal to confirm it decreases correctly; compare the final size with a manual count of remaining nodes.

Check that when removing a node with two children, you correctly handle the in-order successor promotion: ensure the successor is removed from its original location (and size is decremented there) and not double-counted or left in the tree.
